## Read Length Distribution 
```{bash}
zcat raw_reads.fastq.gz | head -n 40000 | bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' > read_lengths.txt

```

```{bash}

 #FOR EXPLANATORY PURPOSES
# Unzips the raw data and sends the data to standard output
zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz \
# This is a pipe. It sends output from the previous command as input to the next command
  | \
# Here we select only the top 40k lines in the file. This equates to 10k reads. It should be plenty to get some stats
  head -n 40000 | \
# This is a small bioawk program. It prints the name of each sequence followed by its length
  bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' \
# Send outputs to a file called read_lengths.txt
  > read_lengths.txt
```

## Plotting
```{r}

library(tidyverse)

rl_data <- read_tsv("read_lengths.txt",col_names = c("id","length"), show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(rl_data, aes(x=length/1000)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  xlab("Read Length Kb") + ylab("Number of Reads")

#Figure 1: Histogram of read lengths in the mockl nanopore sequencing dataset
```
From this plot it is clear that the majority of reads are between 1 and 50kb in length. A good way to summarise this is the N50 statistic. 

# Calculating read N50
Although N50 is most often used to summarise genome assemblies it’s also very useful for summarising read length distributions. The reason this statistic is useful is because it is unaffected by having a large number of tiny reads and instead places greatest emphasis on the longer reads in the data. 
Let’s calculate the read N50 for our sample of reads. The method we will use to calculate N50 is described by the following pseudo-code

Step 1: Rank all reads from longest to shortest
Step 2: Create a new column with the cumulative sum of read lengths (starting from longest read).
Step 3: Find the read at which the cumulative sum surpasses 50% of the total read volume (ie total sum of all read lengths)
```{r}
total_len <- sum(rl_data$length)

rl_data |> 
  arrange(desc(length)) |>            #rank reads
  mutate(cumsum = cumsum(length)) |>  #cumulative sum
  filter(cumsum>total_len/2) |>       #^ pass 50% total vol
  head(n=1)
```

# Activity 1
 Pick apart and understand the code below
```{bash}
## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   id                                        length   cumsum
##   <chr>                                      <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1 c96c1300-8177-e260-d9bd-2fdf75d0146b_2040  22322 74486252
```
Break up the code in the snippet above.
id: read idenificatino number
length: base pair length of longest read
cumsum: cumulative sum of read lengths
Start by removing all pipes and slowly add them back, looking at the data each time. Make sure you understand what the code is doing.

We see here that the N50 of the individual reads is about 22Kb (length = 22,322). Keep this in mind as we perform assembly. We expect that the N50 of our assembly should be considerably greater than this.

## Chromosome lengths and GC content in the reference data
In DNA, guanine always pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds, whereas adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T) through two hydrogen bonds
G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds instead of two, DNA regions with a higher GC content are more thermally stable and have a higher melting temperature (essential for PCRs involving melting and annealing)

Code for bioawk program calculating GC content and size
Plain text file: gc.awk

Use your gc.awk script to print GC and lengths for the assembly
```{bash}
#Send output to "gc.awk"
cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk

#Send outputs to "assembly.gc.tsv"
cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk > assembly.gc.tsv
```

## Plotting 
GC Content - assembly.gc.tsv
Coverage Depth - assembly_info.txt
```{r}
gc <- read_tsv("assembly_check/assembly.gc.tsv",col_names = c("#seq_name","length","GC"))
info <- read_tsv("flye_metagenome/mock/assembly_info.txt")
```

Joining datasets with key column (seq_name)
```{r}
gc_info <- info |> 
  left_join(gc)
```

Histogram of GC Content values for assembled contigs in a flye assembly of the mock community dataset
```{r}
gc_info |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  ylab("Number of contigs")
```

Filtered data to remove contig with unrealistically high GC content and coverage depth (potentially repeats)
Figure: Coverage and GC Content of assembled contigs in the mock community assembly. Contig lengths are shown through point size
 - compare cotigs with highest coverage to those in bandage
```{r}
gc_info |> 
  filter(GC<0.8) |> 
  filter(cov.<25) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC,y=cov.)) + geom_point(aes(size=length)) + ylab("Coverage depth")
```
